facts.t: Kerala reissued 140 of its 144 ordinances in a single year
facts.d: That was 2021 — three decades after D. C. Wadhwa called re-promulgation a fraud on the Constitution. Central re-promulgation is rare, with only 42 ever reissued; the states are where the practice survives.

facts.t: An ordinance cannot amend the Constitution
facts.d: The power is limited to matters on which the legislature could ordinarily make law. Constituent power under Article 368 is a different power altogether, and no ordinance can touch it.

facts.t: Bihar re-promulgated the same ordinances for years
facts.d: The state kept a set of ordinances alive through repeated re-issue rather than passing them into law. D. C. Wadhwa exposed the practice in 1987, and Krishna Kumar Singh finally settled it in 2017 — thirty years apart, on the same state's conduct.

bank.q: With reference to the ordinance power, consider the following statements:
s: It may be exercised only when either House is not in session.
It extends to matters on which the legislature could ordinarily legislate.
It may be used to amend the Constitution.
bank.e: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Constitutional amendments cannot be made by ordinance — that requires the constituent power under Article 368.

bank.q: Which case described re-promulgation of ordinances as a fraud on the Constitution?
o: D. C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar
Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar
bank.e: D. C. Wadhwa (1987). Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) later confirmed the position and added that an ordinance must be laid before the legislature.

bank.q: Which one of the following is NOT correct about the constitutional scheme for ordinances?
o: An ordinance must be passed within six weeks of the House reassembling
Ordinances are judicially reviewable for legislative competence
A Governor may promulgate an ordinance on a matter that should have been reserved for the President
The President may return or reject a proposed central ordinance
bank.e: A Governor cannot promulgate on a matter requiring Presidential reservation — that would let the state bypass the reservation requirement entirely.

bank.q: Match List I (case) with List II (holding):
pairs: 1. An ordinance must be laid before the legislature
2. Urgency is essential; ordinances are not a substitute for regular lawmaking
3. Re-promulgation is a fraud on the Constitution
4. Actions taken under a lapsed ordinance may remain valid
bank.e: A. K. Roy on urgency, D. C. Wadhwa on re-promulgation, Krishna Kumar Singh on laying before the legislature, and the doctrine of past operation on lapsed ordinances.

bank.as: Political difficulty in passing a Bill does not justify an ordinance.
bank.rs: Article 123 contemplates necessity arising from circumstances, not from the absence of legislative majority.
bank.e: Both true and the Reason explains the Assertion. An ordinance reproducing a stalled Bill is treated as the clearest form of misuse.

bank.q: Consider the following as justified uses of the ordinance route:
s: The IIITDM Kancheepuram Ordinance, 2011, closing a temporary legal gap for graduating students.
bank.e: Statements 1 and 2 are justified. The Tribunals Reforms Ordinance is cited as misuse — structural reform introduced by decree rather than in response to a sudden emergency.

bank.q: All of the following are recurring problems with ordinance use EXCEPT:
o: Re-promulgation to keep policy alive without legislative approval
A statutory cap on the number of ordinances per year
Promulgation immediately after a session ends on foreseeable matters
bank.e: There is no cap at all — its absence is listed among the problems.

bank.q: The Land Acquisition Amendment Ordinance of 2014–15 is cited as misuse because it was:
o: Re-promulgated three times while replacement legislation was before Parliament
Issued by a Governor without Presidential reservation
bank.e: Repeated re-promulgation while Parliament was actively examining the replacement Bill — the precise conduct Krishna Kumar Singh condemned.

bank.q: With reference to a lapsed ordinance, consider the following statements:
s: Actions already taken may remain valid under the doctrine of past operation.
Rights conferred survive automatically without being expressly saved.
bank.e: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Rights conferred or taken away may be lost unless expressly saved or re-enacted.

bank.q: Ordinance promulgation peaked in which decade?
bank.e: 196 in the 1990s, against 133 in the 1970s — both periods of coalition instability.

bank.as: Ordinance-making strains the separation of powers.
bank.rs: Legislative power is exercised by the executive, and the resulting laws often reach the courts for validation.
bank.e: Both true and the Reason explains the Assertion — usurpation of legislative function, followed by judicial overload.
